bioghist.head: Biographical Information
bioghist.p: The House of Burgesses was an assembly of elected representatives from Virginia that met from 1643 to 1776. This democratically elected legislative body was the first of its kind in English North America. From 1619 until 1643, elected burgesses met in unicameral session with the governor and the royally appointed governor's Council; after 1643, the burgesses met separately as the lower house of the General Assembly of Virginia. Each county sent two burgesses to the House; towns could petition to send a single representative, as Jamestown, Williamsburg, and Norfolk did. In May 1776 the House of Burgesses ceased to meet, and the Virginia Constitution of 1776 created a new General Assembly composed of an elected Senate and an elected House of Delegates. The House of Delegates was the House of Burgesses by another name. The House of Burgesses is notable for being the training ground of many of America's revolutionary leaders, including George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Richard Henry Lee, and Patrick Henry.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Content
scopecontent.p: Journals of the Virginia House of Burgesses dating 1692-1693 (originals and transcripts), 1702-1718 (transcript), 1742-1749 (original), 1760-1761 (transcript), and 1769-1770 (original). The transcripts consist of manuscript transcriptions of journals, possibly by Library staff, containing both complete and incomplete drafts. The journals are daily records of the proceedings of Virginia's elected lower house covering such topics as financial matters, military defense, military claims, pension requests, public works, religion, land sales (including native lands), property rights, enslavement, and education. The journals include debates, reports, petitions, orders, declarations, and passed laws. An additional Journal, 1773-1776, is available [see LVA Acc. 36808], focusing on the escalating conflict with the royal governor, Lord Dunmore, and Great Britain. The records include debates on parliamentary taxes, non-importation agreements, the Boston Tea Party, and the formation of a Continental Congress.
